title: Once saved, always saved — a Christian can’t lose salvation
objection: If salvation is a free gift of grace through faith, it can’t be lost — otherwise it was wages, not a gift. ‘No one shall snatch them out of my hand’ (John 10:28). A Christian who falls away was never truly saved to begin with.
summary: Scripture warns believers — real believers — that they can fall: ‘lest I myself should be disqualified’ (1 Cor 9:27). The warnings would be theater if falling were impossible. Grace is a living relationship, and relationships can be broken.

response.heading: The New Testament warns Christians, not hypothetical people
response.body: Paul writes to believers: ‘I pommel my body and subdue it, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified’ (1 Cor 9:27). Hebrews warns those ‘who have once been enlightened’ and ‘shared in the Holy Spirit’ that they can ‘fall away’ (Heb 6:4-6). ‘Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling’ (Phil 2:12) is addressed to the saints at Philippi. If perseverance were automatic, every one of these warnings would be God play-acting.

response.heading: ‘No one shall snatch them’ — but sheep can wander
response.body: John 10:28 promises that no outside force can rip believers from Christ’s hand. It says nothing about the sheep wandering off herself. Jesus’s own parables assume it: branches in the vine that bear no fruit are ‘thrown away’ (John 15:6), and Paul tells Gentile believers that if God ‘did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you’ — ‘provided you continue in his kindness; otherwise you too will be cut off’ (Rom 11:21-22). Security from enemies is not immunity from our own choices.

response.heading: ‘They were never really saved’ makes assurance impossible
response.body: The fallback — anyone who falls was never truly saved — destroys the very assurance it promises. If the finally-fallen were never saved, no living Christian can know she is saved rather than self-deceived; assurance becomes available only at death, which is exactly the Catholic position minus the honesty. Catholics hold confident hope: ‘he who endures to the end will be saved’ (Matt 24:13) — assurance with its eyes open.

response.heading: Grace is a marriage, not a transaction receipt
response.body: A gift can be thrown away; a marriage can be betrayed. Scripture describes salvation as a living union — and John speaks plainly of ‘sin which is mortal’ (1 John 5:16-17), sin that kills the life of grace in the soul. That is why Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive post-baptismal sin (John 20:23): if falling were impossible, confession would be pointless. The Church’s teaching is the teaching that takes all of Scripture’s warnings seriously.

simple: The Bible warns real Christians they can fall away — Paul worried about being ‘disqualified’ himself. ‘No one can snatch you from Jesus’ means no enemy can steal you, not that you can’t walk away. Catholics have confident hope, not a guarantee that ignores the warnings.
oneLiner: ‘Lest I myself should be disqualified’ — Paul wrote that about himself. The warnings are real because the danger is real.

title: The Gospels were written too late to be reliable
objection: Mark was written around AD 70, John near AD 100 — decades after Jesus died. That’s decades of telephone game: stories growing, miracles accreting, sayings invented. We have no idea what Jesus actually said or did.
summary: Decades is early by ancient standards — Alexander the Great’s earliest biographies are centuries later. And the Gospels were written while eyewitnesses, including hostile ones, were still alive to object. The telephone game needs a closed room; this was a crowded one.

response.heading: ‘Late’ by what standard? By ancient standards, this is lightning-fast
response.body: Our two earliest biographies of Alexander the Great were written more than 300 years after his death; nobody doubts he existed or conquered Persia. The Gospels land within 30 to 65 years of the events — in living memory. If that gap disqualifies them, ancient history as a discipline collapses.

response.heading: The eyewitnesses were still alive — including the hostile ones
response.body: Paul, writing in the 50s, tells the Corinthians that the risen Jesus ‘appeared to more than five hundred brethren at one time, most of whom are still alive’ (1 Cor 15:6) — an invitation to check. Luke opens by saying he consulted ‘eyewitnesses and ministers of the word’ (Luke 1:2). Legends grow in the dark, after the witnesses die. Christianity’s boldest claims were published in broad daylight, in the city where they happened, while the other side could still answer.

response.heading: The telephone game misdescribes oral cultures — and we have the early creed
response.body: First-century disciples were trained in memorization; rabbis’ students preserved their masters’ words as a discipline, not a party game. And we don’t have to guess what the earliest preaching sounded like: 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 preserves a creed scholars date to within about five years of the crucifixion — ‘Christ died… was buried… was raised… appeared.’ The core was fixed before the telephone could ring.

response.heading: The manuscripts close the gap from the other side
response.body: The earliest Gospel fragment (P52, from John) dates to around AD 125 — within a generation of composition. Compare that to other ancient works, where a thousand-year gap between original and earliest copy is normal. Between early composition and early copying, the window for wholesale invention is vanishingly small.

simple: By ancient standards the Gospels are remarkably early — decades, while eyewitnesses lived. Paul even invited readers to check with the 500 witnesses, most still alive. And the core creed about Jesus’ death and resurrection dates to within about five years of the events.
oneLiner: Alexander the Great’s biographies are 300 years late and nobody doubts him. The Gospels are decades early — with living eyewitnesses invited to check.

title: Did the apostles even exist — or are they legends?
objection: Strip away church tradition and the apostles look like legendary figures — like King Arthur’s knights. We have no neutral, contemporary biography of Peter, James, or John. The early church needed founders, so it invented them.
summary: Paul claims to have met Peter and James within years of the crucifixion — writing to hostile audiences who could check. Josephus, no friend of Christians, mentions James. And nobody invents founders who come across as cowardly, bickering, and slow.

response.heading: Paul met them — and said so to people who could check
response.body: Around AD 50, Paul writes that he ‘went up to Jerusalem’ and spent fifteen days with Peter, and met ‘James the Lord’s brother’ (Gal 1:18-19). He’s writing to churches that included his opponents. If Peter and James were invented, this is a strange lie to tell in public, in living memory, to people who travel to Jerusalem. Paul also lists resurrection appearances to named, living individuals (1 Cor 15:5-8) — ‘most of whom are still alive.’

response.heading: A hostile witness corroborates
response.body: Flavius Josephus, a Jewish historian writing for Rome with no love for Christians, records the execution of ‘James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ’ (Antiquities 20.9.1). Tacitus, equally hostile, confirms Christ’s execution under Pilate and the early Christian movement in Rome (Annals 15.44). The apostles appear in non-Christian sources exactly where you’d expect historical figures to appear: incidentally.

response.heading: Nobody invents heroes like these
response.body: If the early church were manufacturing founders, it would have manufactured impressive ones. Instead the Gospels give us apostles who bicker about greatness (Mark 10:37), fall asleep in Gethsemane, and abandon Jesus at his arrest — with Peter denying him three times. This is the criterion of embarrassment: you don’t invent stories that humiliate your heroes unless you’re stuck with the facts.

response.heading: They died for what they claimed to have seen
response.body: Traditions of apostolic martyrdom are early and widespread — and while details vary, the core is undisputed: the first generation suffered for the claim that Jesus rose. People die for false beliefs they think are true; they don’t willingly die for what they know they invented. Liars make poor martyrs.

simple: Paul wrote that he personally met Peter and James, to audiences who could check. The hostile historian Josephus mentions James. And the Gospels portray the apostles as cowardly and slow — nobody invents embarrassing founders.
oneLiner: Paul named names to hostile audiences who could check — and nobody invents founders who abandon their leader and bicker about greatness.
